ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory identity verification and screening of all directors, officers, shareholders, and UBOs against the following: Public Safety Canada's listing of terrorist entities under the Criminal Code; Global Affairs Canada consolidated sanctions list administered under the Special Economic Measures Act and United Nations Act; UN Security Council consolidated list; FINTRAC published guidance and risk-based due diligence requirements under the PCMLTFA; and, as cross-border best practice for Stripe and PayPal payment rails, the U.S. OFAC SDN List. Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs), including foreign PEPs, domestic PEPs, and family members or close associates, require enhanced due diligence, source-of-funds verification, and senior management approval prior to incorporation proceeding. Ongoing transaction monitoring and a six-year record retention period apply under the PCMLTFA and its regulations.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Ontario Business Registry (online portal accessible at ontario.ca/page/ontario-business-registry) together with the NUANS name search system operated through accredited search houses; the federal alternative is Corporations Canada and its Online Filing Centre, which governs if a federal CBCA corporation is selected instead.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Under the Business Corporations Act (Ontario), a corporate name must be expressed in English, French, or both, and shall be set out in Roman (Latin) script. A name may include numerals, a distinctive element, a descriptive element, and a legal element (e.g., Inc., Corp., Limited, or Incorporée). Names in non-Latin scripts require a certified transliteration or translation into English or French. The name must not be confusingly similar to an existing corporation, trade name, trademark, or a reserved name as determined by the NUANS search, and must otherwise comply with the prescribed distinguishability rules of O. Reg. 62/96 under the OBCA.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: If the proposed name is rejected by the Ontario Business Registry or Corporations Canada, the following administrative path applies: (1) request a written statement of reasons for the refusal from the Director under the applicable registry; (2) where the refusal is based on confusion or non-distinguishability, obtain a revised NUANS report and file a formal request for reconsideration with the Director, including written submissions addressing the confusing similarities and any consent or waiver letters from holders of conflicting names or trademarks; (3) where the refusal involves a sensitive or prohibited token, apply to the competent ministry for prior written approval or adopt an alternative corporate name; (4) if the Director maintains the refusal, appeal by way of judicial review to the Divisional Court of the Superior Court of Justice under the Judicial Review Procedure Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. J.1, within the applicable limitation period; (5) as a practical fallback, incorporate using a numbered name and subsequently file an application for a change of name once the desired name is cleared.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Permissible for this helpdesk/SaaS industry with conditions. The registered office must be a real, physical street address in Ontario and may not be a post office box alone; it must be capable of accepting service of process. A licensed virtual office or registered-agent arrangement with mail forwarding is accepted by the Ontario Business Registry, provided that statutory records and the ISC register are maintained and accessible at the registered office or at another location in Ontario. The customer support helpdesk business model does not require a physical storefront or premises-based license. Under the OBCA director-residency rules, at least 25% of the board, or a minimum of one resident Canadian director where the board has fewer than four directors, must be resident Canadians; therefore, a non-resident founder must either appoint a qualifying Canadian resident director or use a professional corporate director service to maintain commercial substance and regulatory compliance.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low; approximately 5% annual probability for a low-risk, non-licensed SaaS helpdesk with no physical premises and no regulated activities. The probability rises to approximately 30-40% only upon a compliance trigger event, such as a FINTRAC report anomaly, a Canada Revenue Agency audit, client complaints, or a director residency or registered office compliance inquiry.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) – My Business Account portal and Non-Resident GST/HST Registration portal (https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/e-services/cra-login-services.html)
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A non-resident corporation providing digital services to Canadian recipients must obtain a Business Number (BN) and a GST/HST account by filing Form RC1 or using the CRA's online non-resident registration portal. The applicant must provide certified foreign articles of incorporation, proof of foreign tax residence, director identification, and the foreign tax identification number. For a Canadian-incorporated Business Corporation, incorporation is completed under the Canada Business Corporations Act or Ontario Business Corporations Act, and the CRA automatically issues the BN upon incorporation; registration for GST/HST can be added separately. No minimum capital is required, and a Canadian registered office is necessary for Ontario corporations.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Canada does not have a check-the-box regime comparable to the United States. Available elections include: the closely related corporations election under section 150 of the Excise Tax Act (to eliminate GST/HST on certain intercorporate supplies); the joint venture election under section 273 of the Excise Tax Act (permitting election into a GST/HST joint venture for qualifying activities); and the associated corporations election under the Income Tax Act (for allocation of the small business deduction). Hybrid mismatch rules follow the OECD recommendations and are contained in the Income Tax Act; no elective hybrid mismatch neutralization is available.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: GST/HST (Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax) - Value-Added Tax system
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 in worldwide taxable supplies (for non-residents, taxable supplies made in Canada over any trailing 12-month period; the small supplier threshold is CAD 30,000)
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada does not mandate real-time fiscal clearance, digital stamping, or government pre-clearance of invoices. A GST/HST registrant must issue an electronic or paper invoice containing prescribed information (vendor and recipient identification, description, tax amount, and GST/HST rate). Mandatory electronic filing through the CRA's GST/HST NETFILE or the GST/HST E-Filing service applies to registrants whose annual taxable supplies exceed CAD 10 million; all other registrants may file electronically or on paper. No API-based fiscal device connectivity is required.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Zero-rated export treatment is available under sections 21 to 29 of the Excise Tax Act. Goods exported from Canada are zero-rated, and services (including helpdesk and cloud SaaS) supplied to a non-resident recipient are zero-rated if the recipient is not resident in Canada at the time the service is performed and the service is not in connection with real property or tangible personal property situated in Canada. The supplier must retain full documentation showing the supply was made to a non-resident and that payment was received in the ordinary course of trade, including contracts, invoices, and evidence of outbound service delivery.
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: The CRA may reassess a GST/HST return within four years (or indefinitely where a taxpayer has made a misrepresentation that is attributable to neglect, carelessness, or wilful default or has committed fraud). If export zero-rating is disallowed, the exporter is liable for uncollected GST/HST, plus compound interest calculated daily at the prescribed rate. Penalties under the Excise Tax Act include a 20% penalty on any net tax evaded, and gross negligence penalties of up to 50% of the additional tax payable. Criminal prosecution is possible for wilful evasion, with fines up to CAD 200,000 or imprisonment of up to two years, or both.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada) as monetary authority and, since the Retail Payment Activities Act regime, as the regulator for registered payment service providers; Department of Finance Canada retains exchange-rate and financial-sector policy authority; Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) supervises Schedule I banks; Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC) enforces the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA); Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) administers cross-border currency declaration forms.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The Canadian dollar is fully convertible under the Currency Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. C-52). Canada operates an open capital account with no exchange-control legislation, no prior-approval regime, and no formal distinction between current-account and capital-account transactions. Profit remittance is unrestricted at the FX level; the only fiscal impediment is Part XIII non-resident withholding tax of 25% on dividends paid to non-residents, treaty-reduced (e.g., 5% for a US corporate shareholder holding at least 10% of voting shares under the Canada-US Tax Convention). A Helpdesk SaaS corporation may invoice and hold USD/EUR, convert currencies at its own treasury discretion, and repatriate funds without central-bank approval. Compliance duties are transactional only: FINTRAC electronic funds transfer reporting for remittances of CAD 10,000 or more, and CBSA physical currency declaration for cash or bearer instruments crossing the border.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: None. Canadian federal and Ontario law impose no statutory surrender timeline, no mandatory conversion ratio, and no repatriation deadline for export or SaaS service receipts. Revenue generated under ISIC 6201 / NAICS 511210 may be retained indefinitely in foreign currency. The only applicable duty is the PCMLTFA cross-border reporting regime: physical import or export of currency or monetary instruments of CAD 10,000 or more must be declared to CBSA on Form E677, and non-physical wire receipts are automatically reported to FINTRAC by the receiving financial institution without any separate corporate filing.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Rating: Medium-High with legal constraints. Stripe Billing and PayPal Business, the target payment rails, are fully compliant: Stripe Canada settles net SaaS subscription receipts in CAD directly into the Canadian corporate operating account, and PayPal Business Canada operates as a FINTRAC-registered Money Services Business. Wise Business is viable as a multi-currency receivables and conversion utility because Wise Canada is FINTRAC-registered, but it is not a Canadian-chartered bank, holds no OSFI prudential license, and its deposits are not CDIC-insured; therefore it must not be the sole treasury repository. Pure offshore E-Money Institutions without a Canadian FINTRAC MSB registration and without registration or registrability with the Bank of Canada under the Retail Payment Activities Act cannot lawfully access Canadian clearing rails; using such entities for recurring customer-support revenue creates an unregistered-PSP exposure and is rated Low viability.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Mandatory in-person sign-off for most Schedule I banks. At least one director or signing officer, preferably the resident Canadian director required under the Canada Business Corporations Act or the Ontario Business Corporations Act, must attend the selected branch with original government-issued identification and execute the account application, signature card, and FINTRAC identity declaration. Fully remote account opening is offered by RBC, TD, and BMO for simple all-Canadian structures using enhanced video-identity verification, but the presence of any non-resident director or foreign beneficial owner materially increases the likelihood of an in-branch interview. Where remote opening is permitted, the bank requires commission-of-oaths or notarial certification of signature pages, a certified copy of the certificate of incorporation, by-laws, and a board resolution appointing account officers. Recommended posture: appoint and verify one resident Canadian director in person as the principal signing officer and maintain foreign directors as non-signing officers to eliminate recurring branch-attendance friction.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident beneficial owner or director holding directly or indirectly more than 10% of the corporation with no in-person verification
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certified Certificate of Status from Corporations Canada or the Ontario Companies and Personal Property Security Branch; notarized passports and proof of address for all 10%-plus owners; source-of-wealth declaration; 12-month personal and business bank statements; cap table and shareholders register; share subscription agreement; CBCA/OBCA resident-director attestation; and completed international KYC questionnaire of the bank.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Subscription inflows aggregated through Stripe Billing and PayPal instead of direct remittance, creating a third-party-payment-processor money-laundering red flag
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Executed Stripe and PayPal merchant agreements; PCI DSS attestation of compliance; published privacy policy and SaaS terms of service; 12-month subscription revenue forecast with average contract value, churn, and ticket-volume metrics; processor settlement statements; chargeback and dispute history below 0.5%; and the helpdesk platform customer-vetting workflow.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Immediate related-party capital injection within the first 90 days of incorporation with no Canadian operating history
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Board resolution authorizing the injection; share subscription or intercompany loan agreement; funding schedule and intended-use-of-funds memorandum covering cloud infrastructure, payroll, and marketing; W-8BEN-E from the foreign shareholder; foreign corporate registry extract; source-of-funds confirmation; and fair-market-value basis if shares are issued above par value.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Corporation lacks a Canadian tax footprint, payroll, and physical substance at onboarding
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Canada Revenue Agency Business Number (BN) and Ontario GST/HST registration confirmation; registered-office lease or commercial virtual-office arrangement acceptable to the bank; corporate minute book with CBCA-compliant resident director; first fiscal-period financial projections; client letters of intent or active beta agreements; and a statement confirming that the Helpdesk SaaS activity requires no statutory license under ISIC 6201.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Multi-currency outflows routed to foreign cloud-infrastructure suppliers, including jurisdictions at heightened sanctions or ML risk
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Complete treasury flow chart mapping each outbound wire to its supporting invoice; SWIFT UETR tracking log; supplier due-diligence files for AWS, Azure, and API vendors; AML policy statement and designated-compliance-officer appointment under the PCMLTFA if the company ever processes third-party payments; sanctions-screening output; and executed infrastructure agreements proving the outsourced IT nature of disbursements.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Compliant wire protocol: the foreign investor initiates an SWIFT MT103 from its home bank to the Canadian bank using the full beneficiary legal name, Ontario registered address, 12-digit Canadian account format (5-digit transit + 3-digit institution + 7-digit account), and the bank SWIFT BIC (e.g., ROYCCAT2 for RBC). Field 70 Remittance Information must carry the purpose notation: SHARE CAPITAL CONTRIBUTION - CA_CORP / ONTARIO / ISIC 6201 / INV REF CA__CA_ON__CA_CORP. US-origin wires may enter via US correspondent clearing or Fedwire before conversion at the Canadian bank; the bank applies its wholesale commercial FX rate and issues an FX revaluation memo that must be archived with the provisional credit advice as evidence of CAD cost basis for share capital. The receiving bank automatically files FINTRAC EFT reports for all inbound wires of CAD 10,000 or more; no additional corporate filing is required for wire transfers. Physical import of currency of CAD 10,000 or more triggers CBSA Form E677; deliberate wire splitting or structuring to avoid reporting thresholds is prohibited under section 12(1) of the PCMLTFA.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Primary international clearing rail is SWIFT MT103 using the Canadian bank international desk instructions, with the remittance field citing supplier invoice number, purchase order, and the corporate ISIC 6201 reference to prevent payment holds. Payments Canada Lynx provides intra-day high-value CAD clearing for domestic supplier, intercompany, and payroll disbursements. Commercial letters of credit under UCP 600 are permissible and available through the trade-finance desks of RBC, TD, BMO, and CIBC for physical infrastructure imports, though not mandatory for SaaS-only operations. Stripe Billing and PayPal outflows to sub-processors are executed through the providers' automated payout engines and must be reconciled daily against settlement reports. All outbound EFTs of CAD 10,000 or more are reported to FINTRAC by the bank automatically; the company must retain UETR confirmations, supplier invoices, and FX tickets in its GST/HST and corporate tax working files.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable CAD/USD and CAD/EUR outright FX forwards transacted under an ISDA 2002 Master Agreement and Credit Support Annex or the bank standard corporate FX forward agreement
Plain-vanilla European-style FX options on CAD/USD and CAD/EUR for downside protection of USD-denominated subscription revenue
Cross-currency swaps and FX swaps for long-term net investment hedging of USD and EUR treasury balances

Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) are legally permissible under Canadian law but commercially impractical for CAD because the Canadian dollar is fully convertible with a deep deliverable onshore forward market; NDFs are reserved only for exotic cross-currency exposures

Natural hedge overlay: align USD inflows from Stripe Billing and PayPal against USD outflows for cloud infrastructure in a segregated USD sub-account, thereby reducing notional derivative exposure and hedge-accounting complexity under IFRS 9

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing attracts a CAD 100 late fee in addition to the annual return filing fee; failure to file for two consecutive years permits the Director to commence administrative dissolution after notice and publication in the Ontario Gazette.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: No prescribed late fee for the annual return itself; but failure to file for two consecutive years allows the Director to strike the corporation from the register and dissolve it administratively after a default notice and cure period.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within six months after the taxation year-end; for a calendar-year Canadian-controlled private corporation the due date is June 30
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing triggers a penalty of 5% of the unpaid balance plus 1% per full month of delinquency, up to 12 months; interest accrues on unpaid balances and the CRA may use enforced collection measures.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: There is no revenue, asset, or employee threshold for an Ontario or federal private business corporation. A mandatory independent audit applies only to distributing corporations or reporting issuers under Canadian securities law. A private non-distributing corporation may dispense with the auditor appointment and the audit for a fiscal year only with the unanimous written consent of all shareholders.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: Publicly accountable enterprises must prepare financial statements under International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). Private enterprises may elect to use Canadian Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises (ASPE) or IFRS in accordance with the CPA Canada Handbook.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: The corporation must maintain a register of individuals with significant control (ISC register) at its registered office. At least once each fiscal year, the board must review and confirm that the ISC register accurately reflects all individuals with significant control. Any share transfer creating, changing, or ending significant control must be recorded as soon as known and in any event no later than 15 days after the corporation becomes aware of the transfer. The register must remain available for inspection by shareholders and authorized enforcement or tax authorities.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Individuals with Significant Control

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 10,000 – USD 35,000 per annual certified audit for a small or medium private corporation

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 26.5% (combined federal 15% general corporate rate and Ontario 11.5% general corporate rate)
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) small business deduction reduces combined federal and Ontario income tax to approximately 12.2% on the first CAD 500,000 of active business income; SR&ED investment tax credits and Ontario Innovation Tax Credit are available for qualifying software/helpdesk development activities.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (federal and Ontario consolidated filing) submitted electronically via the CRA EFILE/XML portal or online through CRA My Business Account.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual (a T2 return must be filed every taxation year, including a year with nil taxable income)
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Filing is due no later than six calendar months after the fiscal year-end; final balance of tax is due two months after year-end, or three months for a CCPC claiming the small business deduction on taxable income at or below the annual threshold.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Total revenue stream: helpdesk SaaS subscription fees, implementation fees, maintenance and support revenue from all Canadian and foreign clients.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report only Canadian-source business income for a non-resident corporation; allocate revenue through the Ontario permanent establishment formula and exclude income attributable to a permanent establishment outside Canada where treaty protection applies.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Allowable operating expenses: payroll, cloud hosting, software amortization, subcontracting, rent, travel, and third-party payment processing fees (Stripe, PayPal).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Expenses are deductible only to the extent incurred to earn taxable Canadian income; transactions with non-resident related parties must be priced at arm's length and disclosed on Form T106 if the CAD 1,000,000 aggregate threshold is exceeded.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Canadian taxable income after applying non-capital loss carryforwards, prior-year adjustments, the small business deduction claim, and capital cost allowances.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Compute taxable income under Part I of the Income Tax Act using the treaty permanent establishment attribution rules; do not include Part XIV branch tax in this line.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net combined federal and Ontario corporate income tax payable after tax credits and quarterly instalments, including SR&ED and Ontario innovation tax credits.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident corporations generally pay the 26.5% combined general rate unless a specific treaty provision applies; the small business deduction is unavailable unless the corporation qualifies as a CCPC. Branch tax is reported separately on the T2 schedule.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty: 5% of unpaid balance plus 1% per month for up to 12 months (capped at 12%), with an additional 10% penalty for a second late filing; arrears interest accrues daily on unpaid corporate tax and instalment shortfalls; criminal penalties for failure to file apply under Income Tax Act section 238.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% withholding tax under Part XIII of the Canadian Income Tax Act on dividends paid by a Canadian corporation to a non-resident shareholder.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: The 25% statutory rate applies unless a relevant tax treaty provides a lower rate. The non-resident recipient must complete Form NR302 (Application to Reduce Tax Withheld from Interest and Dividends), provide a Certificate of Residence / Foreign Tax Treaty Residency Certificate issued by the treaty partner jurisdiction, and confirm beneficial ownership. If excess tax has already been withheld, Form NR303 should be used to claim a refund within the statutory limitation period.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory rates for both royalties and interest are 25%. Under the Canada-US treaty, interest is generally 0% and royalties 10%; under several other Canadian treaties, royalty withholding is 10% and interest 10% to 15%; reduced rates require beneficial ownership and current treaty residency certificates.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: Form T106 is mandatory when non-arm's-length cross-border transactions exceed CAD 1,000,000 in aggregate in the taxation year; country-by-country reporting is required for multinational groups with consolidated group revenue of at least CAD 750,000,000; contemporaneous OECD-style Local File / Master File documentation is expected for any significant related-party transaction to protect against transfer-pricing penalties.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Ontario and Canada do not apply offshore Economic Substance Regulations. The CRA instead enforces legal substance through the General Anti-Avoidance Rule, the doctrine of sham or colourable transactions, corporate-residence rules based on central management and control, thin-capitalisation restrictions, and section 247 transfer-pricing recharacterisation.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Deliberately understating helpdesk subscription revenue, fabricating deductible expenses, or claiming ineligible SR&ED credits on the T2 return with intent to evade corporate income tax.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Criminal liability under Income Tax Act section 239: fine from 50% to 200% of the evaded tax, a maximum CAD 50,000 fine on summary conviction, and imprisonment up to 5 years on indictment; civil gross-negligence penalty under section 163(2) of 50% of the understated tax plus daily arrears interest.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who signed or directed the false filing are treated as parties to the offence; they may face imprisonment, extradition under bilateral criminal law, Interpol alerts, and civil restitution for any personal benefit received from the concealment.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Interposing a zero-substance offshore IP holding company in a low-tax jurisdiction to receive elevated royalty or service fees from the Canadian helpdesk entity, while the Canadian entity retains the real employees, risk and customers.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: CRA may recharacterise the arrangement under section 247(2), disallow deductions, and impose a 10% transfer-pricing penalty where the adjustment exceeds the lesser of CAD 5,000,000 and 10% of gross revenue; GAAR can eliminate the entire tax benefit from the round-trip structure.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Where the structure is a sham or fraudulent conveyance, courts may pierce the corporate veil; directors may be personally assessed under section 160 for assets transferred out of the corporation, and CRA can freeze or seize personal bank accounts and property.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Collecting GST/HST on helpdesk subscriptions but failing to file remittances, or deducting employee income tax, CPP and EI amounts without remitting them to the CRA.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The corporation is liable for unremitted amounts, statutory penalties, and compounded daily interest; under Income Tax Act section 227.1 and Excise Tax Act section 323, directors are jointly and severally liable for the full unremitted amounts without any requirement of fraudulent intent.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: CRA may assess directors personally, file liens against personal residences, garnish salaries, and oppose discharge in bankruptcy if the failure resulted from the director's own negligence, reckless conduct, or knowing participation.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Accepting recurring payments through Stripe/PayPal from customers on Canadian, OFAC, or EU sanctions lists, or processing payments for prohibited parties without a minimal sanctions-compliance screen; converting high-risk platform revenue into cryptoassets or offshore accounts to avoid traceability.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act, failure to meet AML obligations can trigger administrative monetary penalties up to CAD 2,000,000 and imprisonment for officers in aggravated cases; breaches of Canadian sanctions under SEMA or SIMSA may attract corporate fines up to CAD 25,000,000.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly arrange, direct, or benefit from evasive payment schemes may be charged for money laundering or sanctions evasion, subjected to asset forfeiture, barred from corporate directorships, and restrained from international travel pending criminal proceedings.
